# models.partition { #wdm.models.partition }

`models.partition`

Body-composition partitioning: how much of a mass change is fat.

This is where the model earns its keep relative to the folk formula
"3500 kcal = 1 lb". That rule assumes every pound lost is pure fat. In reality a
mass change is a mixture of adipose tissue at ~9441 kcal/kg and fat-free tissue
at ~1816 kcal/kg -- a factor of five apart -- so the *same* energy deficit moves
the scale by very different amounts depending on what is being mobilised.

Two effects set the mixture.

**Forbes' law.** Fitting body composition across a wide range of adiposity,
Forbes found fat-free mass to be logarithmic in fat mass,

$$
L = 10.4 \ln F + C .
$$

Differentiating and rearranging gives a parameter-free prediction for the fat
fraction of any mass change:

$$
p_{\text{Forbes}} = \frac{dF}{dW} = \frac{F}{F + 10.4} .
$$

The fatter you are, the more of what you lose is fat. At 30 kg fat mass the
prediction is 74 %; at 15 kg, 59 %. This is why the last stretch of a diet is
genuinely harder than the first: not only is maintenance lower, but a larger
share of each lost kilogram is lean tissue, which carries far less energy and so
comes off faster per unit deficit while costing more that you would rather keep.

**Protein intake.** Adequate protein during an energy deficit shifts the mixture
toward fat. Modelled as an additive shift on the fat fraction, proportional to
protein intake relative to a reference of 1.6 g/kg/day.

## Functions

| Name | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [effective_energy_density](#wdm.models.partition.effective_energy_density) | Energy density of the tissue currently being gained or lost, kcal/kg. |
| [fat_fraction](#wdm.models.partition.fat_fraction) | Fat fraction of the current tissue change, in ``[PARTITION_MIN, PARTITION_MAX]``. |
| [forbes_fat_fraction](#wdm.models.partition.forbes_fat_fraction) | Fat fraction of a mass change predicted by Forbes' law, dimensionless. |

### effective_energy_density { #wdm.models.partition.effective_energy_density }

```python
models.partition.effective_energy_density(x, u, p)
```

Energy density of the tissue currently being gained or lost, kcal/kg.

$$
\rho_{\text{eff}} = p \rho_F + (1 - p) \rho_L
$$

Ranges from about 5630 kcal/kg at the lower partition bound to 9290 at the
upper one. Since the rate of mass change is the energy imbalance *divided*
by this quantity, a lean subject on low protein can lose scale weight almost
twice as fast as a fat subject on high protein at an identical deficit --
while losing considerably more muscle in the process.

### fat_fraction { #wdm.models.partition.fat_fraction }

```python
models.partition.fat_fraction(x, u, p)
```

Fat fraction of the current tissue change, in ``[PARTITION_MIN, PARTITION_MAX]``.

Combines the Forbes baseline with a protein-driven shift. Clipping the
result keeps the effective energy density inside physical bounds; without it
an unconstrained ``partition_kappa`` could drive the fraction outside
``[0, 1]`` and produce a negative energy density, which is not so much
inaccurate as meaningless.

### forbes_fat_fraction { #wdm.models.partition.forbes_fat_fraction }

```python
models.partition.forbes_fat_fraction(fat_kg)
```

Fat fraction of a mass change predicted by Forbes' law, dimensionless.
